projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edith Walter was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Today is Monday March 10, 2008 and we're here at the house of Edie Walter. Mrs. Walter was in World War W2 and she's agreed to be interviewed for the Veterans History Project at the Library of Congress. We'll just start back at the beginning, maybe a couple minutes of background and how you came to be in Washington in 1943.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I grew up in Washington, we came here in 1927. My father was appointed to the Interstate Commerce Commission, so that's the reason we landed in Washington. And as happens to most people, we stayed. I graduated from Sweetbriar College [private women's college, Amherst, VA] in 1942 I wasn't quite sure what I wanted to do, so I went down to my father's office and taught myself to type. I had a friend by the name of Bobbie Emmons and she was working at a new agency, the OSS, I wasn't quite sure what that meant. She called me and she said "Edie, come down here. They're hiring like crazy." And I said, "Well, what can I do? I can't do anything." She said "It doesn't matter, just come on down." So I did. Well, it turned out that the fact I had majored in French and minored in Spanish was important, so they hired me, right on the spot. And that's how I got to OSS.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did they give you a typing test to get into OSS?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: No, no typing test. I told them I could type, and that was sort of it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you have a job interview?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I don't remember any details, I just remember I was shocked. I was hired and told to come and started right in. My first job, I was given newspapers from Spain and some from France, and I was to read them and look for train movements. I thought, what is this all about? But anyway, it wasn't until later I realized how important train movements were. In other words, movement of troops, whatever.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: So every day, you were given a paper or two to read, and..

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I would write it down, type up a report. And then they moved me into what they called the Reporting Board. I worked there for Jean Begg, she was a civilian we had a very small room. We were in a temporary building; at 26th and Constitution Avenue, right where Route 66 now takes off no sign of our building [now]. We had a veiy small room. In those days you had a desk with a thing that came out the side to hold your typewriter. Some of them came out on the right and some on the left, so there was a problem arranging the room so that you could get into your desk without having the typewriter in the way. [Laughs] I can remember that Mrs. Begg made a diagram, a diagram of the desks, took it home, and figured out how; so we got it arranged so we could all get in and out.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: How many in the room?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I think there were six of us, maybe five. Every room, of course, had a big safe. Everything was secret. Had to be locked up at night. My desk was located right under the crack in the ceiling and we were on the first floor. And I can remember periodically two men would come in, one would stand on my desk and measure the crack. The problem being that the safe upstairs was over the crack. [Laughs] Some of the joys of a temporary building! Happily the safe never did come down on me. And we received reports from overseas. Mrs. Begg would distribute them and our job was to edit them down, and type them up on ditto, which was very messy stuff. It was purple. You could correct it with a razor blade, if you made a typo, which was sort of fun. I got very good at that. You could make d's into b's, and it was messy. It was in your hair, it was all over you, it was up your nose, in your mouthand terrible stuff on your clothes, but that's what we worked with. And then those reports were disseminated. Mrs. Begg was the one who decided where they should go. They'd go to State Department, Army intelligence, Navy intelligence, whatever; they were distributed throughout the intelligence world.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: So you typed this up on paper which could reproduce itself as many times as ...

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes. You cranked it through a machine, sort of like a mimeograph. It was hot. We had a fan; of course there was no such thing as air conditioning, and of course that helped to blow this mess all over us. That wasn't so good. I do remember at the corner of the hallways we had a dispenser of salt pills, that was... I never had a salt pill. But that was if you had been too hot, too sweaty, you'd need salt

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Otherwise you'd keel over from dehydration?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I guess so.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Were you obliged to take these salt pills or was it only in a desperate situation?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I think it was only in a desperate situation. We had our own cafeteria, it was pretty awful and pretty noisy. The best thing was a Cheese Dream, which was sorta like a melted cheese sandwich with a big blob of jelly in the middle and it was pretty good it was safe. It wasn't all that that bad, but we thought it was bad. If somebody had a birthday, a very special occasion, and your boss would permit it, we could go to the Watergate Restaurant which was right there on the river. We could walk there. Our building was right there you'd have to remember, the brewery was down there. We were right by the Heurich Brewery [former DC beer brewery] which gave a nice odor. [Laughs.] But that's sort of the physical setting of where we were. We worked six days a week. If you wanted a haircut you took annual leave. It was serious business.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: You were impressed with the seriousness of it?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, yes, there wasn't any question; course, everything we worked with was secret. I think I eventually got to where I could handle Top Secret.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Talk about that. Were there security clearances?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: How did you get ranked up [to handle greater levels of secrecy]?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: You worked a while, and eventually as you went along I guess they increased it. I don't know, I don't remember how that worked. You just did it, you know.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Were you fingerprinted and all that?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, yes. I started work at OSS before I had the clearance, believe it or not, and before I had any of the civil service whatever. I remember going down and having a physical. I suppose within a month or so [I was fingerprinted]. You just did what you were told.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Were you sworn to secrecy, did you have to sign things, any oath of some sort?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: We were certainly sworn to secrecy; I don't remember taking an oath; we probably did. They were pretty careful; you weren't to say anything, anywhere. But that was true for everyone, really. You know they had those big signs and Loose lips.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: You couldn't talk to your parents about your work?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I think they just accepted that. That was understood by everyone.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: So you came to work in the OSS in June of and no, it was January of'43.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: The work we were doing was with France and Spain and some from North Africaand the reports would come in from those areas. So when the war was over in Europe [May '45], it pretty well dried up you know, there really wasn't much to do. And I stayed on for a few weeks, and I just thought, "I can't tolerate this any longer."It's pretty hard to sit down there six days a week and have nothing particularly to do. Also, I was still living at homeand whereas other people needed that job a lot more than I did. So I did resign. But I do remember I had to get a doctor's statement that I was resigning because I was exhausted. That's how they let me go which is sort of interesting. And I could not take another job. I think it was six months. So that's why I say it was proper for me to go, rather than someone else who really needed that. I was safe and secure at home. I could afford that

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: During the course of your work, did you get any feedback at all about [the quality of] your work?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Not really, it was just a matter of trust.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Any regular staff meetings?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: No. We just, as I say, we just did what we were told. You always wonder of course where these reports were coming from. Of course, there was no identification of who was sending them and well, there was, but not anything we could understand. It might be a number or letters. We didn't know who was sending it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: On your off hours there was a lot of social interaction between all these people in Washington and Washingtonians. Can you talk about that?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I guess the biggest thing I had there was my work at the Stage Door Canteen, which was located in the old Belasco Theater right there at Lafayette Square. It was right by the Treasury Building and they had been using it for storage, as I understand it. So anyway, it was taken over. I actually started there before I was employed. And the idea there was to entertain the soldiers. They were not only our soldiers but the military from Britain or wherever. They'd come and they'd serve them a sandwich, soft drinks, whatever. And they had it set up with tables, and they had music, either a live band or records. And the soldiers would come in and we were supposed to mosey around and talk to them and dance with them, whatever, just generally entertain them. We were not supposed to leave with any soldier. That was part of the rules. But it was a very nice thing and some of these guys were pretty lonesome. I remember one in particular, obviously from the boondocks someplace. He was stationed out at Walter Reed. He was so lonesome, and shall we say not much of a dancer, and it was a chore [laughs]but it made you feel good. It was fun. That was one fun thing. I remember one time my father was a Chi Psi [men's collegiate fraternity]I don't know how it happened. Anyway he got a letter from somebody that there were a bunch of Chi Psis coming, you know, so he fixed us up mostly went to the movies. 'Course we didn't have cars, we weren't driving, these fellows didn't have cars. So we walked a lot. Which reminds me, coming home from the Stage Door Canteen was sort of interesting because it'd be 10:30, 11 o'clock at night, and of course the city was pretty much blacked out. We had to take the streetcar, then we walked, maybe four blocks. It was kind of scary. We never had a problem, but we were careful, hopped, skipped and jumped; my mother wasn't too fond of that, but we did it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Where were the movie theaters?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: There were several downtown, F Street was the spot. There was the Capitol and the Palace; it was on 15th Street I think. I used to walk across... I lived where we could walk across to the Shoreham Hotel, that was exciting because there'd [be] dancing whatever, live bands; that was exciting. It was really very quiet. Sundays my sister and I would mostly walk, be outdoors. Working six days a week inside is a long haul.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: What time did you have to start work in the morning?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I think we were there at 9 in the morning. And the biggest problem for me was that we lived so far in town that the [incoming] buses would be full. So I got into a little trouble there, because we lived next door to the Saint Nicholas Apartments. There were a couple of fellows there who were army officers and so they offered to take me down in the morning; I had to sign their gas ration cards. That was two cards. Then my sister who worked across town would pick me up at night and she was able to drive so I signed her gas ration card. Then a third guy joined the first two they carpooled. So I signed his. Well, this got me into trouble. The police called me in. Happily my father went to with me; we had to go to the police station and explain how this happened. You can see, I signed a lot of gas ration cards. That's the way it was. Daddy got me off or whatever, it was all resolved. It was scary. I had never been hauled in by the police before. [Laughs] That was a new experience!

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Do you think there was a lot of black market stuff going on in Washington?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, there could have been, I just don't know.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Let's see, what else? My sister and I were the air raid wardens for our area. We had a fairly big house, since we were a family of seven. We had a big sign in the front yard: "Civil defense shelter." In case there was an air raid, people could come to us. My sister and I, we had to take a First Aid course. The thing I remember was, treat for shock and call the doctor. We took the course up at Adams Elementary school; that was exciting. They would have an air raid test [drill]. We would go out, we each had a flashlight covered with a black cloth. You took just a straight pin and made a hole, and that's all the light we had to walk around the neighborhood and make sure there was no light coming from anyone's house. In our house we had a skylight over the stairs, wonderful and Daddy painted it with black paint. I often wondered if someone [removed it]. Yes, we had to be blacked out.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you recall any actual air raids?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: We were theoretically prepared. The drill would be when we went out with our flashlights. The city was sorta blacked out all the time and I know on our street all the street lights were out. It was darkish. They had it so there was some light.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you go on about your normal social life?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, yes, sure. Of course there wasn't a lot. Most of the boys that I knew were overseas. So most of the social life was boys who came from afar, knew someone, say, your roommate in college had a friend who was coming. That kind of thing. So you had a lot of blind dates. [Laughs]

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Any of those memorable in any way?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, there was one, he was sort of memorable, nothing spectacular.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you use your language skills in the Stage Door Canteen?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: No, I don't remember using them. I used them at work, sometimes with reports that came in, in addition to the newspapers would be in another language. It helped.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you follow the progress of the war in the newspapers?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: A little bit. I didn't have much time to read the newspapers, we got most of it at the movies. It was hard because we really didn't know what was happening. The only thing I can remember being sort of fascinated by was the fact that the Germans were setting up these V-rockets and that they could use to send something over to England to think that this could be. That's one of the few things I remember picking up from the reports, that you could send something. At that time that was pretty exotic. So I had an inkling about these train movements to Germany that seemed odd but we didn't know anything. Sarah Rouse:: Did any of this fall into place afterwards?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: It was pretty much a jumble. It was hard to know. I wish I could remember more, but it was a lot of stuff coming in. I can remember, too, going down sometimes on Sunday. There were two reasons to go on a Sunday. One would be if something important had come in, and the other one was if someone had left the safe open and we'd put everything in the safe, so there was nothing in your desk drawer, other than blank paper. It was pretty tight.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Were the other young women in the office working on what you were?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, I think we were all doing pretty much the same thing.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Do you remember what papers and Paris, Madrid, other cities?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Mostly I think the Paris papers, Madrid, some from places I'd never heard of. We also got some from Belgium. Sarah Rouse:: Spain had just had its own Civil War. Did this have any bearing on what you were doing?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I certainly knew about it but I don't remember anything specific. We used to envy and wonder about our agents and whether we ever saw them. Because they would come back, of course. "Who was that guy walking down the hall?" Or "Who was that woman?" Because of course they had women agents. You never knew. "Who was that person? I don't remember seeing him before." You couldn't really ask. You learned to keep quiet; you learned not to ask questions.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you ever see a colleague get dressed down for being too curious or talking too much?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, I had a friend who got dressed down for being at a cocktail party where her boss was also present. He thought she was talking too much. I have no idea what she was saying. The funny part was, he accused her of having drunk too much and she didn't drink at all. So that was not the reason. But you know, if you get to chatting, it took a little effort to be very careful what you said. I don't know what she said but I don't think she gave a big secret away. But anyway, she got called on the carpet for that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you get to know people in other departments?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: No, were pretty much tied to our desks, there wasn't a lot of... [chitchat], you know. It was hard work when I think back on it, but we didn't think anything of it. It was just what you did.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you have any interest in building your work in the OSS into a career?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, what I did do, when I left OSS, they had classified me as an editorial analyst. So I thought, "Oh, I guess I'm an editor." So when I started looking for a job, I looked for editorial jobs. So I ended up at the American Automobile Association, in their editorial department [laughs]. So yes, it launched my career. After I left the OSS I had to wait 6 months. I remember I applied for one other job, which I did not get. Then I answered an ad for the American Automobile Association. Had a wonderful time there for several years, worked part time, eventually quit.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Can you talk about these documents, which say you got a salary increase, from $1620 per year to $2000

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I started at $1400 something, I think... I ended up at $2000.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: I see from this, you started as "Assistant clerk," then you got to "Clerk" then "Editorial analyst" and promotions?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, I had a professional rating.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: I notice these are signed by Catherine Pepe, and June McPeak, do you know...?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I have no idea who they were, they were just part of the Civil Service.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Were you aware of and William Donovan [OSS head]?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I don't remember anything more what's been put out. But the headquarters were up on the hill there, which used to be the...the Navy had that...the Naval Commandant...a big brick building. He pretty much stayed up there. We didn't see him very much. I think, Mrs. Begg's immediate boss, I think his name was Childs. I did work for him a few times; he dictated to me on the typewriter and here's somebody who taught herself to type! The secretary didn't seem to be able to do that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: And you taught yourself [to type] at your dad's office?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, I took my sister's typing book and learned office skills, in my father's office. He and two other gentlemen had an office. They were basically retired, had some...stuff they did, but they taught me to answer the phone properly, and I taught myself how to type.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: In college, did you have expectation of having to do anything like this?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I never thought about it. I was just having a good time. My sisters had all gone to college and then they went to secretarial school, that was sort of the thing people did. I just did it myself. Of course, when I was a senior, they were recruiting for the Navy, particularly. I had one roommate who did go into the Navy. And I thought about that, but somehow I didn't want to do that. I don't know why. I think I was ready to come home for a while. And that roommate, her father was in the Navy, and I remember Pearl Harbor distinctly because he was captain of the Helena, which was at Pearl Harbor. So she sat up all night long. You have to remember we didn't have communication in those days, so she didn't know if he had been hit, or what. The ship was hit but he survived. He was OK. But it was dramatic.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: You knew there was a lot of danger, obviously.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, yes. We had lots of friends whose brothers were sent overseas. I remember one friend from college, she was married, and her husband was one of the early ones killed. So we were well aware of the horrors of war. We were at war and and we lived in Washington, DC, which we thought was pretty vulnerable. There were U-boats off the coast. Yeah, we did know all that. So it was scary. I mean, this was serious business, no question about it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you have to wear any kind of uniform, or office attire?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: No, the only thing I remember, and I think it was so silly, but at the Stage Door Canteen we had to wear little aprons to show we were hostesses. And of course we all had tags, name badges, for the office and everything and we had to wear it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Was the Stage Door Canteen for all ranks?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, yes, it was for anybody. You didn't see too many officers, they had better things to do. [Laughs] I do remember one British guy was there, and I had a terrible time getting rid of him. He followed me out and got on the bus. I also had a friend who was there, who married one of the fellows she met there, in spite of the fact that we weren't supposed to. But anyway, she did, so...

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: I guess wartime mixes things up a lot...sometimes in a good way.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: You were the youngest of your siblings?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: And your parents lived in Washington. Did they feel obliged to take in renters?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: We didn't have room, but they participated, I remember, in different ways. Of course, Mama had to struggle to get food on the table. I don't remember enough about the rationing to be able to say what we were allowed, but... I remember many of what I'd call skimpy meals. And of course I remember we had oil for the furnace, and Daddy ran out, we ran out. We had three days in January with no heat. Happily we had two fireplaces, but those of us who lived on the 3rd floor were cold. You could see your breath. Getting a shower and cleaning up was pretty hard. So we had to learn to keep that furnace down so that we wouldn't run out.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Back to work. In the cafeteria, was that covered in your salary?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, we paid for that. Not exorbitant. Of course, all the prices, it's so hard to remember [looks at old newspaper, reads] Calvert's Old Drum for $1.19. Here's Taylor's wine for 69 cents. It's hard to adjust your thinking.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: We were looking earlier at a picture you have, of an evening out with a couple of friends.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: [Looks at picture] Well, this was my roommate from college. And she had met Sidney Kent who was a longtime friend of mine. And she thought he was pretty neat, and he thought she was pretty neat, so she came up from North Carolina to visit. And so we went out, the three of us. I don't know whether I had a date that night or not. I don't seem to have, at least he's not in the picture. I guess it was just the three of us. And we went to the Lounge Riviera, which was very popular. And it was located in the Hotel 2400 on 16th Street. I don't know whether it's still there or not. I can't remember. It was a very "in" spot. They had this, you know how they do in these places, they take your picture and you eould buy it, or not. Apparently we bought it!

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: It looks like a nice club, with leather banquettes.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, we thought it was really neat. Of course we are smoking our cigarettes. And I notice my drink is dark, and it was a Cuba Libre, we thought that was really neat. Coke and rum. It could have just been a plain Coke, but I have a feeling it included rum.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: And you're smoking.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, yes. Cigarettes were big. Even when I was in college, the cigarette companies would come around and pass them out. And the soldiers got cigarettes all the time.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: There's one other document I wanted to look at. Your efficiency rating at the OSS. Can you tell how that came to be determined?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, I think they just talked to the boss. I don't remember anything [about that], I seem to have gotten one. [It covered the period] from October 18, 1944, from March 31, '45. That's when I resigned-May?

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Here's the interpretation. You got an excellent rating. It's still done this way.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, it was civil service. At that time the Civil Service Commission was located in what is now the [Smithsonian's National] Portrait Gallery. Here's a certificate. It says I "honorably served" and it's dated the first day of October 1945, and it has William Donovan's signature. [Another document, reading and] "the Stage Door Canteen, the American Theater Wing War Service Incorporated ... presents this certificate in deep appreciation of one year's loyal and outstanding volunteer service." I'm not sure but that I served more than a year, but that's okay.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: And I see a letter ...

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: ... Mr. Shepardson,I guess that's head of SI [Whitney Shepardson, Chief of OSS's Strategic Intelligence Branch]. Dated 28 September '45. [Reading:] "at the conclusion of the wartime effort the Office of Strategic Services I should like to take this opportunity of expressing to you my personal appreciation and that of the agency as well for your contribution to the success of our wartime activity during the two-and-a half years of your association with..."

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: It looks like it's signed by Mr. Shepardson.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: So, you know, it was a fun thing to do.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: I'm going to stop this [tape] and flip it over. We may speak a little bit longer (other side of tape)

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: You remember saving up for shoes?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, I wanted a pair of... They were very "in." I think it took a lot of ration stamps. I don't know but I can just remember saving for those.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Did you get them?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Uh huh!

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: What was the shoe store?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I can't remember. But before the war I remember getting my school shoes at Richies [?], next to.... They're now out here at Mazza Gallerie. They used to be next to Woodies' [Woodward and Lothrop, department store formerly on 11th and G, NW in downtown DC].

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Those are ration stamps..for anything?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: See, they're not designated, they're all numbered.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: You paid instead of cash?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: You took your ration book, and whatever you were buying, it said you had to have... And they would take 'em out. Here's [reading] "war ration book number 3. Office of Price Administration."

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Every adult got a set of ration stamps?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I guess that's the way it worked.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: In pictures of wartime, all the women seem to have nice shoulders ...shoulder pads?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, yes, everything had shoulder pads. Of course, we didn't have nylons, you've heard that story. I had a pair that I'd saved from college days. We had...in fact it was hard to get any kind of stockings. We used to paint a line up the back of our legs to make it look like the seam and all stockings had seams. Meat was rationed rather severely, I think because...I did take one vacation. We took the train from here to Chicago. I went with a friend. And then to Vancouver, British Columbia, then on board a small ship and went up the inner passage to Juneau, Alaska. And the reason we went there was, she had a friend who had a husband who was in the Coast Guard, stationed up there. That was the motivating force. But we were blacked out. The boat was blacked out. [At night] we had to stay down below and everything was blacked out. But it was a fun trip, and exciting. We stayed in the Marinaut/Barinot [?] Hotel in Juneau, and we had steak and roast beef every night! It was just heaven on earth! But of course, no fresh stuff, canned beans, and...you know. Coming back, I can remember we had to change trains in Minneapolis, Minnesota. I don't quite know why Minneapolis, but... And we went to a a hotel there and we all ordered a great big green salad! [Laughs] We were deprived! Of course, riding the trains was something else again, because we had only the old, old cars. I can remember going on that trip, when we went from Washington to Chicago. We sat up all night. It was raining, hard, and coming in the window. It was a mess, next to me. So we went into the ladies room, whatever you called it, and got as many paper towels as we could and stuffed them in the window, but it didn't do much good. But it was...we had the old, old cars to travel in. Of course, everything was packed. I remember going to New York and sitting on my suitcase between the cars.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Servicemen had priority?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: You didn't mind sitting on your suitcase between the cars?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I was young then, sure, that was the way it was.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: When you went to Alaska, that would have put you on the West Coast. Did things seem any different, say, the orientation toward Japan, the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Not really. The boat we were on was very small, and I don't have any memory of it being much different. It was certainly wartime, no question.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: It must have been nice to be able to take a little time off work.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, yes, annual leave. As you can see, I ended up with 184 days [probably meant 184 hours] so that was the only really vacation that I remember taking. The rest of the time we were working.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Your parents did not have any objections to your working?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I think they thought that's what you were supposed to be doing. They certainly thought that when you got out of college you were supposed to... go to work. I paid a small...I don't remember how much... I paid Mom and Dad a little rent money, and I was... I think I also had to pay...we had a servant, and I think her salary was $7 a week. But she did some of my laundry. So I had to add a little for that. Momma thought it was veiy important that we should do that, and I think Daddy did, too.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Do you have any thoughts on the idea that the war enabled women to do work they had not done before?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: There's no question it opened up all sorts of possibilities. We all know about Rosie the Riveter, that sort of thing. Yes, because up until that time, you were supposed to teach school, or be a secretary, do a job of that sort. That was pretty much... We were excited. We were winning that war, by gum! Someone asked me one day, "Did you ever think you'd lose?" I said, "Well that's the dumbest question, of course we didn't think we'd lose." It never crossed anybody's mind. The event of Pearl Harbor just galvanized everyone. We've had 9/11 and although it galvanized us, it was a different thing. Very different. Of course, the war in Europe had been going on. OSS had been started. I think Donovan was called in.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Before Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, I think it was....

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: I see you're looking at the book, Sisterhood of Spies: The Women of the OSS, by Elizabeth Mcintosh.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: It's mostly about the ones who were spies, who went overseas. Of course there were a lot of jokes. My and husband-to-be was in India. They use to get a kick out of the OSS women and looking for information or a prospective husband. [Reading] "OSS personnel who signed an oath of secrecy" so maybe I did sign one, I don't know. [Reading] "On 18 June 1941 before Pearl Harbor Roosevelt summoned Donovan to the White House to discuss the formation of America's first national intelligence agency." They'd never done this before, it was all new. "Both men felt the United States would soon be drawn into World War 2 and a unified wartime intelligence system serving both military and government requirements was imperative." They were trying to figure out how to do it, I mean they were ... It was all brand new and there was lots of jealousy or tension or whatever you want to call it, between the Army intelligence, Navy intelligence, State Department intelligence, all vying for information... It was an interesting time. Yes, you can imagine forming this thing from nothing! And they used to kid about... Sometimes it was called Oh So Social because there were a lot of socialites came to work for OSS -

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Like Julia Child?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Like Julia Child, and my boss Mrs. Begg, she was Dutch in origin, and married a guy from the State Department, but normally would not have been doing that kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: It required a sort of social ease, I think?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Yes, Mr. Childs, he came from some university, he was a professor. They came from all sorts of different backgrounds.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: When you think back on it, being in the OSS, what are your thoughts?

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: It was a marvelous experience for me. I don't know, it's hard to say what else, we were very proud of it. As I say, we felt strongly about it and we were winning that war, we were doing our part; that was a very big part of it. As I say, all our contemporaries, boys, men we should call them, were out fighting. So, by gum, we were doing our part. I mean, that was the sense of it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Many people think it must have been special to be there in the early days of the OSS, and even though you weren't privy to the entire big picture, it must have been special experience.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: I think it was. I probably just sort of took it for granted a little bit, you know. It was special, I was very proud of it, and I did well.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: We're coming around to the end, at least for now I wonder if there's anything final you'd like to say

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, I don't have anything special. I think it's a privilege to be able to record it like this. It's fun to think that it is still important. It's a long time ago, you know, and you sort of forget.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: I feel privileged to be let in on it.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, it was fun and we enjoyed it. Perhaps it is important for people to realize what we did.

sp.speaker: Sarah Rouse
sp.p: Thank you for contributing to the public record, for me and for those who come after.

sp.speaker: Edith Walter
sp.p: Well, thank you. I've enjoyed it.
